title: Rotational Motion & Angular Momentum
summary: Rotation parallels linear motion: angular position, velocity, and acceleration, with torque $\tau=rF\sin\theta$ as the rotational force and moment of inertia $I$ as rotational mass. $\tau=I\alpha$, rotational KE is $\tfrac12I\omega^2$, and angular momentum $L=I\omega$ is conserved.

angular acceleration.plain: Rate of change of angular velocity.

torque.plain: The rotational effect of a force.

concept_sections.heading: Rotational kinematics
concept_sections.explanation: Angular quantities mirror linear ones: $\omega=d\theta/dt$, $\alpha=d\omega/dt$, with the same constant-$\alpha$ equations. Link to linear motion by $v=r\omega$, $a=r\alpha$.

concept_sections.heading: Torque
concept_sections.explanation: Torque $\tau=rF\sin\theta$ measures a force's turning effect — larger with more force, a longer lever arm, or a perpendicular push.
math_steps: Find the force and its distance from the axis.
Maximum when the force is perpendicular.

concept_sections.heading: Moment of inertia and $\tau=I\alpha$
concept_sections.explanation: Moment of inertia $I$ plays the role of mass in rotation, depending on how mass is distributed. Newton's second law becomes $\tau=I\alpha$.

concept_sections.heading: Rotational energy
concept_sections.explanation: A spinning body has $KE=\tfrac12I\omega^2$. A rolling object has both translational and rotational kinetic energy.

concept_sections.heading: Conservation of angular momentum
concept_sections.explanation: With no external torque, $L=I\omega$ is constant. Reducing $I$ (pulling mass inward) speeds up rotation — the skater effect.
math_steps: Solve for the new spin rate.

real_world_examples.title: A figure skater's spin
real_world_examples.scenario: A skater pulls in their arms and spins faster.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Angular momentum $I\omega$ is conserved, so smaller $I$ means larger $\omega$.

real_world_examples.title: Opening a door
real_world_examples.scenario: You push far from the hinges.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A larger lever arm gives more torque for the same force.

real_world_examples.title: A rolling ball down a ramp
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Its energy splits between translation and rotation, so it's slower than a sliding block.
